verses.translation_literal: A Maskil of Asaph. Why, God, have you rejected [us] to perpetuity? Does your nose smoke against the flock of your pasture?
verses.translation_dramatic: A song for the wise ear, of Asaph. Why, God? Why have you thrown us away, and for so long it feels like for ever? Your anger is smoking, a fire that will not die down, and it burns on the very flock you feed.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens not with praise but with one word, 'Why?', and it is spoken to a God addressed as Elohim, with no covenant name. Play it as a cry, not a debate. The superscription is 'Maskil of Asaph': a Maskil is probably a skilful or instructive song, and Asaph names a guild of temple singers, so this is liturgy, meant to be sung in a congregation, not a private complaint.

The KJV 'thine anger smoke' hides the body. The Hebrew says אַף, 'nose', and the verb is 'smoke': the ancient picture is of a furious person whose breath steams from the nostrils, as Rashi, Radak and Meiri each note. The same idiom runs through the Bible, 'his nose burned' for anger. The KJV also adds 'us' and 'thou' where the Hebrew has only 'have you rejected'; the object is felt, not stated. 'Flock of your pasture' is the shepherd image that the whole psalter loves (Ps 79:13, 100:3), and it sets the tone: the enemy is not the first problem; God's own silence is.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'your nose'; by metonymy 'your anger', because anger shows in the nostrils. The verb 'smoke' keeps the body picture alive.
'You have rejected, cast off'; the same verb is used of God abandoning his altar in Lam 2:7.
'For perpetuity, for ever'. It returns in vv. 3, 10 and 19, and links the complaint to the question of how long it will last.

verses.translation_literal: Remember your congregation [which] you acquired of old, [which] you redeemed, the tribe of your inheritance; Mount Zion, this [one] you have dwelt in it.
verses.translation_dramatic: Remember them: the people you gathered to yourself in the first days, the people you bought back, the tribe that is your own portion. Remember this mountain, Zion, where you chose to make your home.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first plea is 'remember', and in the Bible remembering is an act, not a thought: it means to act on a bond. Three words of ownership follow, each a business word. 'Acquired' (קנה) is the verb of buying, used of the exodus in Exod 15:16; 'redeemed' (גאל) is what a kinsman does to buy back a relative from slavery or a lost field; 'inheritance' is the family land that cannot be sold away. The speaker argues from God's own property rights: you paid for us, you cannot let us be burned.

The KJV 'rod of thine inheritance' is a literal rendering of שבט, which means both 'rod' and 'tribe'; the ancient hearer felt both, the tribe as the rod of rule. Traditional translations also smooth the final clause. The Hebrew is clipped, 'Mount Zion, this, you dwelt in it', with a pointing 'this' (Rashi reads זה as 'which'). It sounds like a voice pointing across the ruins at the hill itself. Radak and Meiri take 'this' as a hint that the psalm is sung in the place it describes.

philological_notes.note: 'Your congregation', the people as an assembly gathered at an appointed place; the same family as מוֹעֵד in vv. 4 and 8.
'Rod' or 'tribe'. Ibn Ezra reads 'the tribe that is your inheritance' and also considers a construct chain with Mount Zion.
Redeem as a kinsman: a family duty to buy back what was lost. Radak and Meiri refer it to the exodus.

verses.translation_literal: Lift up your steps to the ruins of perpetuity; everything the enemy has done evil in the sanctuary.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rise. Lift your feet and walk to the ruins that look as though they will stand for ever. See it all: everything the enemy has wrecked in the holy place.
verses.directors_commentary:
God is told to get up and walk. The speaker treats the divine presence almost physically: 'lift up your steps' is a summons to a god who has been sitting still, as Radak and Ibn Ezra compare to 'Arise, LORD' (Num 10:35). The scene is an inspection tour through a burnt site, with the guide pointing at each ruin. KJV 'perpetual desolations' is fair but loses the sound: משֻּׁאות is a rare word for ruin, and Rashi ties it to שאיה, 'devastation'.

The last clause is syntactically twisted: 'all [that] the enemy did evil'. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David read it as inverted word order, 'every enemy who did evil in the sanctuary'. The KJV hides the difficulty by inserting 'even all that', which turns an unfinished gasp into a tidy sentence. Play it as a voice that chokes: the list of damage is too big to finish. The word 'sanctuary' is simply קֹדֶשׁ, 'the holy', the place set apart.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'your steps, your feet'. Rashi alternatively hears 'your throbs of anger' from וַתִּפָּעֶם (Gen 41:8); the plain sense is feet.
'Ruins, devastations'; a rare plural linked to שׁוֹאָה and שָׁאִיָּה (Isa 24:12).
'Did evil, did harm'; the Hiphil of the root of 'bad'. The verb is placed before its subject in a way that commentators call inverted.

verses.translation_literal: Your adversaries roared in the midst of your meeting place; they set up their signs [as] signs.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your enemies roared. They roared in the very room where your people came to meet you. And they planted their own emblems there, hung up their own signs as if the place were theirs.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the enemy is a lion: שאג is the verb of a lion's roar (Amos 3:8) and is used elsewhere of God himself. The soldiers fill the room with victory noise. The word for 'meeting place' is מוֹעֵד, the same word as for the appointed festivals; the ancient audience heard a place where Israel and God meet on appointed days (Rashi quotes Exod 25:22, 'I will meet you there'). KJV 'congregations' blurs the place into a crowd.

The last two words repeat a single root: 'they set their signs [as] signs'. The KJV 'ensigns for signs' keeps the echo, but 'ensigns' is a guess: אוֹת can be a military standard, a pagan emblem, or an omen. Rashi and Radak read it as Nebuchadnezzar's divination (Ezek 21:26, 'he looked at the liver'), and Metzudat David adds the bitter irony that the enemy calls the omens true. Keep the repetition alive when speaking: the mockery is that they have made their own sign of victory and call it a sign.

philological_notes.note: The roar of a lion, here of an enemy occupying the sanctuary; Radak links it to the sound of a festival crowd, Lam 2:7.
'Your appointed meeting place' from 'to appoint, meet'; the same word as 'festival', which is why Ibn Ezra explains that places and times of meeting share one name.
'Their signs [as] signs': a repetition of one root. Signs may be standards, idols or omens.

verses.translation_literal: It was known, like [one] bringing upward, in a thicket of trees, axes.
verses.translation_dramatic: It looked like this: men lifting their axes high over a thicket, and the blades coming down into the wood.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the one verse in the passage that no translator fully trusts, and it is worth telling the actors so. The Hebrew is a string of fragments: 'it was known', 'like one bringing', 'upward', 'in a thicket of trees', 'axes'. The KJV makes 'a man was famous' of the first word, which is a guess and a poor one; ASV and BBE both read it as a picture of woodcutters, which fits the next verse, where the same tools smash the carved panels. Play it as a camera shot: a forest, blades raised.

The tradition splits sharply. Rashi and Malbim read it of the enemy: the axes hit the gates, and, says the Talmud (Sanhedrin 96b, as Rashi cites), the wood swallowed the blades. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David read the thicket as the cedar forest where Solomon's builders worked, and the lifted axe as an act of worship: the point is that those who built the temple were honoured, and now the same tools tear it down. The word 'axes' is קַרְדֻּמּוֹת, a woodcutter's tool, and 'thicket' סְבַךְ is the tangle where Abraham's ram was caught (Gen 22:13).

philological_notes.note: 'It was known / made itself known', a Niphal; the commentators disagree on who is known and by what.
A tangle of branches, the thing in which something is caught (Gen 22:13). Rashi hears the wood entangling the blades.
Axes, woodcutters' tools.

verses.translation_literal: And now its engravings altogether, with axe and crowbars, they hammer.
verses.translation_dramatic: And now the carved work, all of it, every panel and every flower in the wood, they hammer down together with axe and iron bar.
verses.directors_commentary:
'And now' sets the earlier craftsmanship against the wreckage. פִּתּוּחִים are the engraved and carved work of the temple, the cherubim, palms and open flowers cut into the cedar walls and overlaid with gold (1 Kings 6:29); Radak and Metzudat David point out that the gold was on those carvings, which is why the soldiers hammer them. The verb הלם is the heavy blow of a hammer, used of Jael's tent peg (Judg 5:26).

The KJV 'carved work', 'axes and hammers' is roughly right but loses the rare tool names. כַּשִּׁיל is a hatchet; כֵּילַפֹּת, found nowhere else, is glossed by Rashi, quoting Dunash, as an Arabic loanword for a carpenter's tool, and Radak as a wooden tool like an axe, so 'crowbars' is a plausible guess, not a certainty. Ibn Ezra also reports the opinion that it comes from a root meaning to peel. The sound is the point: the clank of unfamiliar words as the soldiers strip the temple like a building site.

philological_notes.note: Engraved or carved work, as in the signet engravings of Exod 28:11. The suffix points back to the sanctuary.
A hatchet, found only here; the Targum Jonathan on Jer 46:22 uses it for 'axes'.
A hapax legomenon, a carpenter's tool. Rashi (after Dunash) calls it Arabic; Radak a wooden tool; Ibn Ezra offers a link to a root for peeling bark.

verses.translation_literal: They sent your sanctuary into the fire; to the ground they profaned the dwelling of your name.
verses.translation_dramatic: They put the torch to your sanctuary. They razed the dwelling where your name lived, down to the ground, and made it common.
verses.directors_commentary:
The idiom here is 'send into the fire', a verb of sending used for setting a thing alight (Judg 1:8). The KJV 'cast fire into' reverses it: the sanctuary itself is what is sent into the fire. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David wonder whether the order is inverted ('sent fire into'), but the plain text is stronger and more terrible: the building is thrown to the flames.

The second line is deeper. 'The dwelling of your name' is Deuteronomy's theology, in which God does not sit in the building but causes his name to live there; the enemy therefore does not only destroy a house, he profanes (חלל) the place that carried the name. The root of 'profane' is related to 'common', not sacred, and Metzudat Zion ties it to חֻלִּין. 'To the ground' can go with either verb; ASV and KJV place it with pulling down, which Meiri also takes as the walls thrown to earth. Say it slowly: the holy made ordinary.

philological_notes.note: 'They sent [it] into the fire', the idiom for arson. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read it as 'sent fire into'.
'They profaned, made common', the opposite of sanctifying; Metzudat Zion links it to חולין, the ordinary.
'Dwelling of your name': God's name, not God himself, is said to dwell in the sanctuary.

verses.translation_literal: They said in their heart, "Let us oppress them together." They burned all the meeting places of God in the land.
verses.translation_dramatic: They did not even say it aloud. They said it in the dark of their own hearts, one mind among them: "Let us crush them, all together." And then the fire went from place to place, from one meeting ground of God to the next, until there was not one left standing in the land.
verses.directors_commentary:
The enemy's speech is spoken in the heart: this is a plan, not a shout, and the actors should play it low and shared. The verb is a single word, ninam, with the pronoun "them" fused on, and the word is hard. Read as yanah, 'oppress, wrong', it gives YLT's "Let us oppress them together", which is the sense of the Hebrew root; the KJV's "destroy" is a guess at the force rather than a translation of the verb, and the ASV's "make havoc" does the same. Rashi and Metzudat Zion hear a different word, nin, 'rule', so the speakers become 'their rulers' acting with one purpose; the Targum and Meiri hear 'offspring'. The sound is ambiguous on purpose for a modern ear, and the director should know the actor is choosing.

The KJV's "synagogues" is an anachronism. Mo'adei-el are the 'appointed places' where God was met at the appointed times, and the line points to every sacred meeting place in the land, not to a building type that did not yet exist. Metzudat David reads them as the places set aside for the LORD, the house of prayer and the house of study. Radak narrows it to the Temple alone. Note "in the land": the burning is everywhere, not only at Jerusalem.

philological_notes.note: Most simply 'let us oppress them' from yanah (as in Radak, who ties it to the wronging of body and property, and as YLT renders it). Rashi reads 'their rulers' and Meiri 'their offspring', which would make the line a report rather than a plan. The translation keeps the verb sense and flags the doubt.
'Appointed places of God', places of meeting at the appointed times. The phrase is rare, so the exact reference (the Temple, or local gathering places) rests on the commentators.

verses.translation_literal: Our signs we have not seen; there is no more a prophet, and not with us [one] knowing until when.
verses.translation_dramatic: Their signs stand on the walls. Ours? We see none. No prophet speaks any more, and there is not one man among us who can tell us how long.
verses.directors_commentary:
The word 'signs' came back from v. 4 with a different owner: 'their signs' stood on the temple; 'our signs' are gone. Ibn Ezra notes the reversal. In the ancient Near East a sign could be a miracle, a prophetic token or a message from heaven; the people are describing silence in all three forms, which the Malbim lists. Metzudat David and Radak read it as the signs of redemption; Rashi as God's promised signs through his prophets.

The next claim, 'there is no more a prophet', is the heart of the grief. In Israel prophets were how the people knew where they stood with God, and without one no one can say how long the punishment will last. The KJV 'knoweth how long' is accurate, though the Hebrew is an abrupt 'until what?', a half-question cut off, as Metzudat Zion notes by comparing Ps 79:5. Medieval commentators who place the psalm in the Second Temple period (Radak, Meiri) think the end of prophecy after Malachi is meant; the verse itself says only that the voice has stopped.

philological_notes.note: 'Our signs': God's tokens to his people. Ibn Ezra reads it as the exact reverse of 'they set their signs'.
'Until what?': a short form of 'until when?', as in Ps 79:5.

verses.translation_literal: Until when, God, will the adversary taunt, will the enemy spurn your name to perpetuity?
verses.translation_dramatic: How long, God? How long will the enemy sneer? Will he go on spitting on your name for ever?
verses.directors_commentary:
The question from the end of v. 9 ('until what?') is now asked in full: 'until when?' It is a ritual cry of lament in many psalms (Ps 6:3, 13:2). The shift is important for staging: until now the speaker has told God what has been done to the sanctuary; now the complaint turns to what the enemy says about God, to the insult to his name, the same word 'name' as in v. 7.

The two verbs are paired: חרף is to taunt, to mock with sharp words, and נאץ to spurn, to treat with contempt (Metzudat Zion calls it 'scorn'). The KJV 'blaspheme' for the second is too churchy: it makes the enemy a heretic. The Hebrew shows a victorious soldier mocking a defeated god, and the point of the cry is that it is God's reputation that is at stake, not only Israel's. Metzudat David and Meiri add that the taunt is the claim that God lacks the power to save. Notice the return of 'for ever' (לנצח) from v. 1: the opening plaint and this one bracket the first half.

philological_notes.note: 'He taunts, reproaches', to throw words at someone.
'He spurns, despises'; Metzudat Zion glosses it as contempt. The KJV 'blaspheme' is a theological gloss.

verses.translation_literal: Why do you draw back your hand, even your right hand? From the midst of your bosom, finish [them].
verses.translation_dramatic: Why? Why do you hold it back, your hand, your right hand, folded away in the fold of your robe? Draw it out. Draw it out and finish it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The image is of a man whose hand rests, hidden, in the front fold of his garment, and so cannot strike. The prayer is a reproach: the God who once raised the arm now keeps it tucked away. Play the first half as a question and the second half as a command, pressed out almost through the teeth.

The two hands need care. Radak says "your hand" is the left, so that "and your right hand" completes the pair, and Ibn Ezra likewise takes the first as the left hand, as though both hands were named. Meiri instead hears one idea doubled, 'your hand and your right hand' as a doubling of language. Either way the effect is emphasis: the whole of God's power is being withheld. The KJV "even thy right hand" has weakened the "and" into an apposition and so hides the doubling or pair.

The last word is obscure. Kalleh is an imperative, and the KJV's "pluck it out of thy bosom" and the ASV's "consume them" supply an object the Hebrew does not give. Rashi takes kalleh as 'drive out', 'cast it out of your bosom and fight your enemies', citing Exodus 11:1; Meiri takes it as 'hold back', the reverse; Radak offers 'destroy the enemy from the midst of your bosom', that bosom being the Temple. The Hebrew allows each of these, and the director should choose one for the actor.

philological_notes.note: The bosom or the front fold of a garment, where a hand can be tucked. Radak adds that someone who keeps his hand in his bosom does no work, as the lazy man does. A variant spelling is marked here by the Masoretes (Ketiv and Qere), without change of sense.

Imperative of kalah, 'bring to an end'. Whether it governs the hand ('finish it', i.e. use it) or the enemy ('finish them') is not settled by the verse; Rashi reads 'drive out' (Exod 11:1), Meiri 'restrain'.

verses.translation_literal: And God [is] my king from of old, doing acts of salvation in the midst of the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And yet God is my King, he has been my King since the beginning, the one who works deliverance in the very heart of the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice turns on one small word, the 'and' (ו) at the start, which the KJV renders 'For' and the ASV 'Yet'. It is a hinge: after eleven verses of complaint, the speaker recalls what he knows, which sets a new stage direction. Slow down and drop the pitch. The first word is 'God' again, but now with 'my king' beside it: the king is the one who fights for his people, and the claim is a reminder, almost an accusation, that a king who is silent has not changed his office.

The verse echoes v. 2: 'of old' (מקדם) is the same word as 'of old' (קדם) there, and the thought moves from God's purchase of the people to God as the king who acts. 'In the midst of the earth' can be read as 'in the centre of the earth' or, as Radak says, in the middle of the enemy's own land; Malbim distinguishes salvation by nature from miracles done below. Meiri adds that the claim is that God is publicly known through Israel's deliverance. The KJV 'working salvation' is plain; the Hebrew has the plural, 'saving acts', one deliverance after another, and the list that follows in vv. 13–17 shows what is meant.

philological_notes.note: 'My king from of old': God's kingship is traced back to before the sanctuary; the same word 'of old' as in v. 2.
A plural: 'acts of salvation, victories', not one deliverance but a series.
'In the midst of the earth'; Radak takes it as even in the enemy's own land, Malbim as miracles done below on earth.

verses.translation_literal: You — you split apart the sea by your strength; you shattered the heads of the sea-monsters upon the waters.
verses.translation_dramatic: You, and no other: it was you who tore the sea in two with your strength. The great deep, the one the nations feared, you split like a broken jar. And the heads of the monsters that lived in it, you shattered them where they floated on the waters.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker stops pleading and starts reciting, and the pronoun is the point: 'you, you' — the emphatic אַתָּה opens verses 13, 14, 15, 16 and 17 like hammer blows, the answer to the enemy axes of the previous verses. In Israel's world the sea (יָם) is not scenery; Canaanite myth, known from Ugarit, has Baal fight Yam and the many-headed serpent Lotan, and Mesopotamia has Marduk splitting Tiamat. The psalmist borrows that picture and gives all of the victory to YHWH alone. Traditional readers take it as the Red Sea (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri), with Pharaoh and Egypt as the monsters (Rashi cites Ezek 29:3); either way the claim is that the chaos-power was broken by YHWH, which is why the loss of the Temple does not mean the sea has won.

KJV 'didst divide' softens פוררת, which means to shatter, crumble or break apart, the verb for the earth 'splitting' in Isa 24:19 (Metzudat Zion). KJV also writes 'dragons' for תנינים; the word is a sea-monster or great serpent, the same word as in Gen 1:21. Note the plural 'heads': this is a multi-headed beast, as in the Ugaritic texts.

philological_notes.note: A strong verb of breaking into pieces, not the gentle 'divide' of the KJV. It is used of the earth splitting open in Isa 24:19, as Metzudat Zion notes.
Sea-monsters or great serpents. The plural 'heads of' pictures a many-headed beast. The commentators read it as Pharaoh and his officers, with Ezek 29:3 as the proof.

verses.translation_literal: You, you crushed the heads of Leviathan; you gave him [as] food to a people, to tziyim.
verses.translation_dramatic: You. It was you who crushed the heads of Leviathan, and gave it as bread to a people, for the people of the dry places.
verses.directors_commentary:
Leviathan is the many-headed sea monster of the old Canaanite stories, whom Baal, in the Ugaritic texts, defeats; here the psalm gives the victory to the LORD alone, and the monster becomes his meat. That is polemic: the sea-powers worshipped by the neighbours are a carcass in God's hands. Note the plural "heads": the creature is broken head after head, and the actor can give each its own blow. The opening "you" is stressed again, as in the preceding verses.

The tradition reads Leviathan as Pharaoh, as in Rashi on this verse, and Metzudat David specifies his officers. The KJV's "gavest him to be meat" has the old sense of 'food', and not the modern sense, so it is correct but easy to mishear; "to the people inhabiting the wilderness" is an interpretation, not a translation. The Hebrew says only 'to a people, to tziyim'. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David take tziyim as desert-dwellers, the people who walked the wilderness after Egypt; Rashi takes it as 'companies, bands', as in Numbers 24:24; Ibn Ezra offers sailors, or those who live on the coast. BBE's "fishes of the sea" has no support in any of them. Keep the strange word strange in the literal layer, and let the actor choose.

philological_notes.note: A rare plural. Rashi: 'companies, bands' (cf. Num 24:24, tziyim miyad kittim). Radak, Metzudat David and Meiri: dwellers of the desert, from tziyah 'dry land'. Ibn Ezra: sailors, or coast-dwellers. The translation leaves it unglossed in the literal layer.
The sea monster, here with plural heads. Rashi and Metzudat David identify him with Pharaoh (Isa 27:1, Ezek 29:3).

verses.translation_literal: You — you cleaved spring and torrent; you — you dried up rivers ever-flowing.
verses.translation_dramatic: You split the rock, and out of it came spring and torrent. You, too, turned the rivers dry, the rivers that never fail, until the riverbeds lay open under the sun.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the same hand does the opposite thing in the same breath: it breaks open water where there was none, and it dries up water where there was always plenty. The poem is building to its argument that the one who reverses nature at will can reverse Israel's fortunes.

The verb בקע ('cleave') is used for both spring and torrent, a zeugma: strictly one cleaves rock, and the spring flows out. Radak and Meiri read it as a figure that names the result for the act. Traditional readers take the springs as the water from the rock in the wilderness (Ex 17:6) and the dried rivers as the Jordan at flood (Josh 3:15), as Rashi does. KJV 'mighty rivers' is fine, but the Hebrew אֵיתָן is a technical word for a stream that flows all year, the opposite of a seasonal wadi, so these are not merely large but perennial rivers.

philological_notes.note: Perennial, never-failing (of a stream); also 'strong, permanent'. Radak notes the construct form makes it a noun, 'rivers of permanence'.

verses.translation_literal: To you, day; also to you, night; you — you set firm a luminary and sun.
verses.translation_dramatic: The day is yours. The night, also, is yours. You fixed the lamp of the moon in its place, and the sun, and they have kept their roads ever since.
verses.directors_commentary:
From the battlefield of the waters the poem rises to the clock of the sky. Day and night are not neutral time; they belong to someone. In a world where the sun and moon were gods (Shamash, Sin, Yarikh), the poet says: these are tools, set in place by YHWH. 'To you, day; also to you, night' is a legal formula of ownership, and the words 'to you' are repeated for each half.

KJV 'the light and the sun' reads מָאוֹר as an abstract 'light'. The word is a luminary, a light-bearer; Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David take it as the moon, the 'lesser light' of Gen 1:16, and Ibn Ezra explains that it comes first because the verse just spoke of night. The verb הֲכִינוֹתָ is 'you made firm, you set in place', from the root of כון (a base, a stand). KJV 'prepared' is a little vague; the sense is 'established on a firm base'.

philological_notes.note: A luminary, a light-giver: not 'light' as an abstract. The tradition takes it as the moon (Gen 1:16), set before the sun after 'night'.
To set on a base, establish firmly; Metzudat Zion links it to the base and stand of the root.

verses.translation_literal: You, you set all the boundaries of earth; summer and winter, you, you formed them.
verses.translation_dramatic: You set the borders of the earth, every one. Summer and winter: you shaped them, you and no other.
verses.directors_commentary:
The long hymn of "you" reaches its last turn. Verses 13 to 17 keep returning to the same pronoun; here it appears twice, once at the head of the verse and again just before the final verb. The object is fronted: "summer and winter" comes first, and then the emphatic "you" stands before "you formed them", so the sentence lands on the verb of the potter, yatsar, the word used of shaping clay. Let the actor put the weight on that verb.

Why summer and winter next to the borders of the earth? The ancient reader saw both as limits fixed by God: the land has edges, and the year has two faces, the dry hot season and the rainy cold one. For a farmer in Judah these were not weather but the rhythm on which bread depended. Rashi takes the verse as the promise of Jeremiah 5:24, that God has not changed the order of the years for his people. Radak adds that each region differs from the next, and Ibn Ezra that when it is summer in one place it is winter in another. The KJV's "set" and "made" flatten two different verbs, natsav 'make stand', and yatsar 'form', and lose the craftsman image.

The point of the whole run, from verse 12 on, is the argument: the God who sets the boundaries of the earth can still move his hand.

philological_notes.note: 'You made stand', 'you set up': the word of a boundary stone or a pillar, which fits "boundaries".
'You formed them', the potter's verb (Gen 2:7), so the seasons are shaped like a vessel. The plural suffix refers to summer and winter.

verses.translation_literal: Remember this: an enemy has reproached, YHWH, and a foolish people have spurned your name.
verses.translation_dramatic: Remember this, LORD. An enemy has jeered at you. A people with no sense, no fear, has spat on your name.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turn. After five verses of 'you, you, you', the imperative arrives: זְכָר, remember. The logic is that the one who owns day and night, summer and winter, is the one being mocked, so the insult touches him more than the people. A prayer in the ancient Near East works as a petition to a patron: you have the power, you have the reputation to protect, so act.

KJV 'that the enemy hath reproached' adds 'that', turning a plain command into a subordinate clause; the Hebrew has two bare statements after 'this'. KJV 'foolish' softens נָבָל. The word is not 'silly' but morally dead: the נבל of 1 Sam 25 (Nabal) and Ps 14:1 ('the fool says in his heart: no God'). KJV 'blasphemed' for נאצו is stronger than 'spurned' in modern English; the verb means to treat with contempt. The Malbim gives a neat reading: the fixed order of nature, which the psalm has just praised, is exactly what makes the fool say that the world runs by itself.

philological_notes.note: A person who is a moral fool, one who denies God by acts and not only by words (Ps 14:1). Stronger than KJV 'foolish'.
To treat with contempt, spurn. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'disdain'; KJV 'blasphemed' is stronger than the Hebrew.

verses.translation_literal: Do not give to the beast the life of your turtledove; the life of your poor do not forget forever.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not hand a wild beast the soul of your dove. Do not forget your poor ones, the life that is theirs, not now, not ever.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two pictures, a dove and a predator, put the weakness of Israel in one image. The turtledove (תֹּר) is the offering of the poor (Lev 5:7), a small, defenceless bird; the beast is the empire. The structure is a pair: 'do not give' and 'do not forget', both with אַל.

The word חַיַּת is the crux. It can be 'beast' (construct, 'the beast of ...') or 'company, band' (Rashi, Radak and Metzudat Zion cite 2 Sam 23:11 and 13, 'the band of Philistines'). So KJV's 'multitude of the wicked' follows the second reading and adds 'of the wicked', which is not in the Hebrew; ASV 'wild beast' follows the first; BBE's 'hawk' is a guess. The Hebrew repeats חַיַּת in the second colon with a different sense, 'life' or 'company' of your poor. KJV's 'congregation' follows Rashi and Radak, who read it as a company. I keep the repetition as the poem has it.

philological_notes.note: Either 'wild beast' or 'band, company', with the same noun used a second time in the verse. Rashi and Radak cite 2 Sam 23:11, 13 for 'band'.
A turtledove, the poor man's sacrifice. Rashi cites the dove's faithfulness to its mate as an image of Israel's loyalty; this is the commentator's reading.

verses.translation_literal: Look to the covenant, for the dark places of the land are full of the settlements of violence.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look at the covenant. Look, for the dark corners of the land are filled, and every hiding place has become a house of violence.
verses.directors_commentary:
The poet asks God to look at an agreement, not just at suffering. The covenant is the legal ground of the plea: God has bound himself by oath, to the fathers (Rashi, Radak), and the contract is the claim. The Hebrew has the article, 'the covenant', the one known to both sides.

The second half is very compressed. מַחֲשַׁכֵּי־אֶרֶץ, 'dark places of the land', may mean hiding places in the countryside, or the lands of exile where Israel lives in darkness (Radak). נְאוֹת is from נָוָה, a pasture or settled dwelling, as in 'pastures of shepherds' (Ibn Ezra), so the line turns a word for a safe home into a home of violence: even the places of shelter now shelter violence. KJV 'habitations of cruelty' follows this; 'cruelty' is a little soft for חמס, which is the violence that wrongs people and cries to God (Gen 6:11).

philological_notes.note: Pastures or dwellings, the word for a settled and safe home; here, a home of violence. Ibn Ezra compares 'pastures of shepherds'.
Violence that wrongs another; the sin that ended the world before the Flood (Gen 6:11). KJV 'cruelty' is weaker.

verses.translation_literal: May the crushed not return humiliated; may the poor and needy praise your name.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let no one crushed by their enemies walk away from you in shame. Let the poor and the needy be the ones who praise your name.
verses.directors_commentary:
The petition is about reputation again, this time the reverse of the enemy's insult in verse 18: there the fool spurns the name; here the poor are to praise it. In the ancient Near East a petitioner who left a god or king unheard was shamed, and the shame fell on the patron as well. The poem says: don't let that happen.

The Hebrew verb is plain: 'may he not return', a jussive with a singular 'crushed one', the single supplicant. 'Return' means to go home from the sanctuary or from the king's presence with nothing, as Rashi and Radak read it. KJV 'oppressed' for דַּךְ is acceptable but loses the picture: the word is from דכא, to crush, as in a mortar. KJV 'ashamed' is also fine for נִכְלָם. Three words for the poor stand together: 'crushed', 'poor' (עָנִי) and 'needy' (אֶבְיוֹן). The poem has just used 'your poor' in verse 19; these are the same people.

philological_notes.note: Crushed, one beaten down, from the root of 'to crush' (as in a mortar). Stronger than 'oppressed'.
A standard pair for the poor, the lowly and the needy, the ones the Psalms say God hears.

verses.translation_literal: Arise, O God, plead your plea; remember your reproach from a fool all the day.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rise, O God. Stand up and plead your own case. The cause is yours, and it has been yours all along. Remember how you are mocked, how the fool pours scorn on you, hour after hour, all the day long.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a courtroom summons spoken to the divine judge, and the actor should play it as an urgent, almost impatient call. 'Arise' is what a judge does when he takes his seat to hear a case, and the verb 'plead' (ריבה) comes from the same root as its object, 'your plea' (ריבך): literally 'contend your contention'. The wordplay turns the whole lament around. The people have spent the psalm describing their own ruin, but here the case is no longer theirs; it is God's. Radak and Meiri hear the same logic: if God will not act for the people's sake, let him act for his own, because the people are attacked precisely for trusting in him.

The KJV 'plead thine own cause' gets the sense, and 'the foolish man' keeps the singular. What it changes is the grammar: the Hebrew has a plain noun phrase, 'remember your reproach from a fool', and the KJV, followed by ASV and Webster, recasts it as a clause, 'remember how the foolish man reproacheth thee'. The Hebrew is blunter: the reproach itself is the thing God is told to remember, as one might hand a judge an exhibit. The 'fool' (נָבָל) is not stupid but morally and religiously dead: someone who acts as if God does not exist or does not matter, as in Psalm 14:1. 'All the day' (כל היום) is better than the KJV's 'daily', which sounds like a routine; the Hebrew describes insult without a pause, from dawn to dusk.

philological_notes.note: A verb and its own noun side by side: 'contend your contention'. The lawsuit language makes God both judge and party, and the repetition should be audible in performance. English 'plead your plea' keeps it; 'plead thine own cause' loses the echo.

'Fool' in the sense of a person who has no fear of God and no moral sense, not one lacking intelligence. The singular is collective or representative of the enemy. Malbim stresses the shame of being reproached by such a person.
'Your reproach': the insult aimed at God, not at his people. Rashi glosses it with גִּדּוּפֶיךָ, 'your blasphemies'.

verses.translation_literal: Do not forget the sound of your opposers, the uproar of those who rise against you, going up continually.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not forget the voice of those who stand against you. Do not forget the roar of those who rise up against you, a roar that never stops climbing.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm closes on a sound, not on a promise: a roar that does not stop and goes up, with no reply. The last word is תָמִיד, 'continually', and the poem ends in the same unresolved state in which it began, with a question about 'forever' (v. 1). The effect for an actor is to end on open air, with no 'Amen'.

The Hebrew is more precise than the English of KJV. KJV 'increaseth' turns the verb עֹלֶה, 'goes up', into a rising crescendo; the Hebrew says the noise goes up, as smoke or a cry goes up to heaven, so the enemy's uproar is imagined as reaching God's ear (Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David say it goes up before God). KJV 'the voice of thine enemies' for קוֹל צֹרְרֶיךָ is fine. KJV 'tumult' for שְׁאוֹן is right: the word is also the roar of the sea and of an army. Notice that after verses on the sea monsters, the word for the enemy's noise is the same word used for the sound of the sea (Ps 65:8), a last echo of chaos, now in human form.

philological_notes.note: A roar, tumult, the noise of crowds and of waves; used for the sea in Ps 65:8, so the enemy's noise echoes the chaos-waters of the first half of the psalm. Metzudat Zion glosses 'humming, murmur'.
'Goes up': a participle for ongoing action, the noise rising before God. KJV 'increaseth' is an interpretation.
